Experience replay

An agent's experience arrives in order: this step looks almost like the last one. A network trained on it in that order fits wherever the agent is now and forgets the rest. DQN stores experience in a replay memory and trains on random samples from it instead.

An agent sweeps slowly from one end of a corridor to the other and back. Each step it sees one noisy target for the state it is in. Two identical networks (Lesson 64, 16 units) learn from the same stream with the same number of updates and the same batch size of 32. Online trains on the 32 most recent samples. Replay trains on 32 drawn at random from its memory.

To isolate the effect of ordering, the targets here are fixed noisy values rather than TD targets, as in Lesson 64's demo.

The maths

DQN stores each transition $e_t = (S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1})$ in a memory $\mathcal{D}$ that holds the last $N$ of them. Each update uses a minibatch $B$ drawn uniformly from $\mathcal{D}$:

$$\boldsymbol\theta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\theta + \frac{\alpha}{|B|} \sum_{(s,a,r,s') \in B} \big[y - Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta)\big]\, \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta).$$

A minibatch update only reduces the error averaged over whatever distribution the batch comes from. Write that distribution $d_t$ and, as in the demo, let the target at state $s$ average to $U(s)$. Then the expected update is a step down the gradient of

$$\tfrac12 \sum_s d_t(s)\, \big[U(s) - \hat v(s, \boldsymbol\theta)\big]^2 .$$

For the online learner, $d_t$ covers only the few states the agent just passed through, so each step reduces the error there and nothing pins down the rest. That is catastrophic forgetting. For replay, $d_t$ is spread over the last $N$ steps, which covers the whole corridor once $N$ spans a full sweep. Shrink $N$ and replay turns back into online learning.

Replay also reuses data. If one transition is stored per step and one update of $|B|$ samples happens every $u$ steps, a transition stays in a full memory for $N$ steps, during which there are $N/u$ updates, each picking it with probability about $|B|/N$. So each transition is used

$$\frac{N}{u} \cdot \frac{|B|}{N} = \frac{|B|}{u} \text{ times on average.}$$

In DQN, $|B| = 32$ and $u = 4$: every transition is learned from about 8 times.

The price: replayed transitions were generated by older policies. Only an off-policy method can learn from them as they are, which is why DQN is built on Q-learning, whose target $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ does not depend on which policy chose the actions. Replay is one more reason DQN sits inside the deadly triad of Lesson 65.

Later work samples surprising transitions, those with large $|\delta|$, more often: prioritised experience replay (Schaul et al., 2016).
